column1: # Classical Arabic, the language of the Qur'an and early Islamic poetry
# (7th–8th centuries), in its standard phonemes: emphatics tˤ sˤ dˤ ðˤ,
# pharyngeals ħ ʕ, q, x, ɣ; jīm is d͡ʒ; vowel length kept.
# Nouns and adjectives are given in their pausal form, without case vowel
# or nunation (kalb, bajt, madiːna): the form the spoken dialects continue.
# Verbs are perfect stems, the 3rd masculine singular without its final -a
# (katab "write"); the perfect endings are the agreement slots.
# Broken plurals and the root-and-pattern system are not modelled: each
# word is a fixed stem, and plurals take the sound feminine plural -aːt.
# Hand-written from standard dictionaries (Lane; Wehr) and grammars
# (Wright; Fischer). Concepts left out are coined in Arabic's own sounds.

column2: The Arabic of the Qur'an and the early caliphate: emphatic and pharyngeal consonants, three vowels long and short, verb-first clauses, a definite article.
Lane, Arabic–English Lexicon; Wehr, Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic; Wright, A Grammar of the Arabic Language — simplified by hand
